name: Diego Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cover the farms and little hamlets out past the reservoir, so most of my day is driving. I've got my grandad's old Ford Fiesta, and I do maybe sixty miles a day between five or six clients. First is Mr Hargreaves, who's eighty-eight and lost a leg to diabetes, so I help him wash and get his prosthetic leg on. I only started eight months ago, after the chicken factory I worked at shut down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old farmers. They don't want fuss, they want you to turn up on time and have a laugh. What wears me out is the petrol, because the agency pays a bit per mile but it never covers it. And I'm still slow at some things, like the hoist for the Bell sisters, so I'm always running late. Rosa and I live at her mum's to save rent, which helps, but it's not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought a computer could do my job anyway. I'm not really one for posting online, so I'd just say it at the pub on a Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay how they are, which isn't great but isn't a disaster. I'm still not earning much and there's only one agency out this way. If I lost this job, the next nearest one is forty minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds, same as now, and try to get quicker with the hoist. I'd stop buying the meal deal at the garage every day and take sandwiches. That's about thirty pounds a week I could keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly, but tight. If AI is mostly hype, I'm still driving sixty miles a day in my grandad's old Fiesta for a wage that barely covers the petrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mileage never covers the petrol. How short are you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe forty or fifty pounds a month. In winter it's worse, because the lanes are slow and I use more fuel. I don't complain to the office, because I'm new and I don't want to be the moaner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does living at Rosa's mum's put any pressure on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. Her mum's lovely, but she likes things her way, and we're in the box room. We wanted our own place by next year, but I can't see it on what I earn.

say: I'd say I never thought a **computer** could do my job anyway.
I'd say it at the **pub**, not online.
think: Things stay how they are, which is **not great** but not a disaster.
There's only **one agency** out this way if I lost this job.
do: Keep doing my **rounds** and get quicker with the hoist.
Take **sandwiches** instead of buying meal deals, saving thirty pounds a week.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, I'm still driving sixty miles a day in my grandad's old Fiesta for a wage that barely covers the petrol.
fieldNote: Diego is short about **fifty pounds** a month on petrol and won't complain.
He lost one job when the **chicken factory** shut, so he knows how fast work goes.
His hope for their **own place** is already slipping away.

steps.text: Keep the morning round starting with Mr Hargreaves
Bring sandwiches from home instead of garage meal deals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't bother me much, because you can't wash someone with software. I'd probably keep my head down and see what happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried about the office using it to plan tighter rotas. They already squeeze the driving times. But the actual washing and dressing would still be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and wait to see what the agency actually brings in. I'm not going to rush to learn some app before I have to. I'd keep taking sandwiches and try to save a bit, but there's not much to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, I suppose. Software can plan my route round the reservoir, but software can't get my client's prosthetic leg on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your day could AI take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota, maybe, and the notes, and phoning families. I do all my notes on paper now and drop them at the office on Fridays. If that went onto an app, I'd struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the agency told you to use an app for everything, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it if I had to, but I'd hate it. I'd probably ask Rosa to show me. She's better with phones than me, she works in a shop and does all the stock on a tablet.

say: I'd say you can't wash someone with **software**, so it doesn't bother me.
I'd keep my **head down** and see what happens at work.
think: The office might use AI to plan **tighter rotas** and squeeze driving times.
The washing and dressing would **still be me**.
do: **Keep going** as normal and see what the agency brings in.
Ask **Rosa** to show me any app I'm made to use.
S1.quote: Software can plan my route round the reservoir, but software can't get my client's prosthetic leg on.
fieldNote: Diego still does his notes on **paper** and drops them at the office on Fridays.

steps.text: Carry on with paper notes until the agency says otherwise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should slow it down. I'm not political, but I'd probably vote for whoever said they'd stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be out of a job by 2031, and I've already been through that once with the factory. The thinking AI would just make the office smaller at first. But the robots would come for the hands-on stuff, and that's all I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could for those three years, maybe a hundred a month if I cut everything. I'd look for another job, but I don't know what, because the factories and farms would get robots too. I'd probably lean on Rosa's mum even longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Like when the factory closed. I've already lost one job to a factory closing, and I'm twenty-seven. A robot doing care would make that twice before thirty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do between 2028, when thinking AI arrives, and 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just work as much as I could and save. Maybe ask for extra shifts while the office is short-staffed. I'd keep an eye out for anything local that robots couldn't do, but I don't know what that would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Rosa do about your plans for your own place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to put it off. Maybe for years. Rosa would be gutted, she's been looking at flats on her phone every night.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and someone should slow it down.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to stop it.
think: I'd be **out of a job** by 2031.
I've already been through this once with the **chicken factory**.
do: Save **a hundred** a month for the three years before robots.
Look for **another job**, though factories and farms get robots too.
S2.quote: I've already lost one job to a factory closing, and I'm twenty-seven. A robot doing care would make that twice before thirty-one.
fieldNote: Diego expects to lose his job a **second time** before he's thirty-one.
He has no clear **next job**, because robots hit his other options too.
He and Rosa would **delay** having their own place for years.

steps.text: Save a hundred pounds a month by cutting every extra
Ask for extra shifts while the office is short
Stay at Rosa's mum's house longer instead of renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that someone should slow it down. But I'd be more careful about saying it, in case I looked stupid if it turned out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gives me a bit more time to save, but I'd still be out by thirty-five. I don't really know what I'd do instead. I'm not the type to go back to college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save harder for the first few years, maybe get my own place with Rosa before it hits. Then I'd wait and see what jobs were still around in 2031. I wouldn't jump early, because I did that once and it didn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not as bad as the fast one. Five years just means I get to watch the robots coming up the lane a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years instead of two change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's slower, so I could see what's coming. But I'd still need a new job at the end of it, and I don't know what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn in those years, even if you don't like new tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe driving something, I don't know. Or farm work with Rosa's uncle, who's got sheep. I'd only learn something if I could see a job at the end of it.

Try to get our **own place** with Rosa before it hits.

S3.quote: Five years just means I get to watch the robots coming up the lane a bit longer.
fieldNote: Diego doesn't see five years as **escape time**, only watching time.

steps.text: Save harder for the first three years
Try to rent a flat with Rosa before robots arrive
Wait to see which local jobs survive past 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, so let's see. I'd probably not say much at all, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I've got time to get somewhere else, but I don't know where. I'd be forty when the robots come. That's a long time from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing care and save what I could. Maybe do my care certificate properly, and think about farm work as a backup. I'd wait to see what other people did before deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less worried. Still there, though. Ten years feels like forever until I picture myself at forty, still living at my girlfriend's mum's, with a robot doing my rounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At forty, with ten years' warning, where do you see yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still in care, I suppose, if there's any left. Or on the farm with Rosa's uncle. I don't really plan that far ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that's not so bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the hoist. I hate the hoist. If a robot did that and I did the talking, that'd be all right.

I'd probably **not say much** at all, at the pub or anywhere.
think: I'd have **time** to get somewhere else, but I don't know where.
I'd be **forty** when the robots come.
do: Keep doing **care** and save what I could.

fieldNote: Diego doesn't **plan far ahead** and would wait for others to move first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of work again before thirty-one with nothing saved. What would help is the agency paying proper mileage now, and someone telling us what jobs are actually going to be left. I don't need a robot. I need someone to tell me what job is safe before I waste another five years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the old farmers. Mr Hargreaves hasn't got any family nearby. If the robots come, he'll have nobody at all.

headlineQuote: I don't need a robot. I need someone to tell me what job is safe before I waste another five years.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** carer who drives sixty miles a day round farms past the reservoir.
He lost his last job when the **chicken factory** shut, eight months ago.
He lives with Rosa at **her mum's** and never uses AI tools.
He goes from **anxious** to alarmed under AGI and doesn't believe extra time saves him.
He'd **wait and see** rather than jump, and his backup is farm work with Rosa's uncle.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be out of work again before thirty-one with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Someone telling carers which **jobs will be left**.
